documents.text:
196 FERC ¶ 61,127
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Before Commissioners:  Laura V. Swett, Chairman;
                                        David Rosner, Lindsay S. See,
                                        Judy W. Chang, and David LaCerte.


ORDER ACCEPTING PROPOSED TARIFF REVISIONS, SUBJECT TO CONDITION

(Issued August 14, 2026)

On March 26, 2026, as supplemented on June 16, 2026, pursuant to section 205 of the Federal Power Act (FPA) and Part 35 of the Commission’s regulations, Tri-State Generation and Transmission Association, Inc. (Tri-State) filed a proposed High Impact Load Tariff (HIL Tariff), which includes a pro forma High Impact Load Agreement (HIL Agreement).  In this order, we accept Tri-State’s proposed HIL Tariff and pro forma HIL Agreement, subject to condition, effective July 16, 2026, and direct Tri-State to submit a compliance filing within 30 days of the date of this order.  
Background
Tri-State is a wholesale generation and transmission cooperative operating on a not-for-profit basis.  Tri-State was formed by its Utility Members (which are distribution electric cooperatives and public power districts) for the purpose of providing wholesale power and transmission services to its members for their resale of power to retail consumers.  Tri-State’s Utility Members are parties to individual wholesale electric service contracts (WESC) with Tri-State, requiring Tri-State to sell and deliver to the Utility Member, and the Utility Member to purchase and receive, all energy and capacity required for the operation of the Utility Member’s system.  However, a Utility Member can procure alternative resources to serve its own load through two Tri-State programs—a self-supply percentage and Tri-State’s Bring Your Own Resource (BYOR) program.  The WESCs require Utility Members to pay Tri-State for wholesale power and transmission service as prescribed by Tri-State’s Class A Rate.  Tri-State serves its Eastern Interconnection Utility Members through a Wholesale Power Contract (WPC) with Basin Electric Power Cooperative (Basin) within Southwest Power Pool, Inc.’s (SPP) footprint.  
Tri-State states that it uses a broad planning system designed to evaluate the incremental growth of load across a large system to develop its Electric Resource Plan (ERP) and ensure it can serve its Utility Member load.  The ERP analyzes Tri-State’s predicted energy and capacity requirements over a 20-year span.  The main component of the ERP is the annual long-term base load forecast that is conducted in conjunction with Tri-State’s Utility Members.  Per Colorado law, the Colorado Public Utilities Commission (Colorado Commission) regulates Tri-State’s system-wide resource planning.  Tri-State explains that the Colorado Commission regulates the ERP under a two-phase process that occurs every four years and includes engagement from stakeholders within Tri-State’s system.  The first phase of the process analyzes generation types and quantities across Tri-State’s system based on a developed expansion plan.  The second phase of the process involves Tri-State’s competitive solicitation for resource bids necessary to satisfy the needs of the expansion plan.  Following the ERP process, Tri-State’s OATT provides for both transmission planning and cost allocation of transmission facilities.  Tri-State states that its transmission planning process is divided across:  (1) the transmission planning group, focused on OATT functions and compliance with North American Electric Reliability Corporation Reliability Standards, and (2) the member system planning group, which works with Tri-State’s Utility Members on changes to their sub-transmission or distribution systems.  Tri-State explains that costs of network upgrades and interconnection facilities on its system are also allocated to Utility Members under applicable OATTs of neighboring transmission providers.
Tri-State explains that its planning processes and assumptions from historical 
data regarding load additions are being challenged by the development of large loads, particularly data centers in the Mountain West.  Tri-State states that it is a 2.5 GW peaking system, and that it has received 31 requests from Utility Members with loads ranging from 45 to 650 MW in the first year and increasing to 300 to 1,600 MW after a 10-year phase-in period.  Tri-State asserts that the projects have planned initial               in-service-dates from 2026 to 2029, and would double Tri-State’s system peak over a 10-year period. 
On August 28, 2025, in Docket No. ER25-3316-000, Tri-State proposed to establish a High Impact Load (HIL) program to address its concerns regarding the rapid growth of large loads.  The Commission rejected Tri-State’s proposal because it represented an “impermissible intrusion on retail rate regulation” and thus was not subject to the Commission’s FPA section 205 authority.  The Commission found that “several provisions of the HIL Tariff require specific terms and conditions of service by a Utility Member to an end-use HIL Customer (i.e., a retail service).”  More specifically, the Commission found that section 3 of Tri-State’s proposed HIL agreement required the Utility Member to set certain requirements for the terms of energy sales from the Utility Member to its retail customer through a Member Contract with High Impact Load (MCHIL).  As examples, the Commission noted that section 3.A.4 of the proposed HIL agreement required the MCHIL to include certain minimum load and energy requirements for retail purchases by the HIL Customer from the Utility Member, that section 3.A.9 imposed monthly caps for retail energy or demand, and that both requirements appeared to dictate certain terms and conditions for retail sales from a Utility Member to its end-use customer.  
The Commission further stated that, “should Tri-State choose to refile a modified version of the HIL Tariff that does not infringe on retail rate regulation, we encourage Tri-State to address, for example, but not limited to, the following concerns.”  
First, the Commission stated that it appeared that Tri-State had not sufficiently demonstrated that the security deposit was appropriately sized to mitigate the risks that Tri-State identified, and that Tri-State had not explained why it is appropriate to round up its cost-based rate in deriving the security deposit.  Second, the Commission stated that Tri-State had not sufficiently explained why the HIL agreement termination provisions would allow Tri-State to terminate a Utility Member’s HIL agreement for reasons beyond the Utility Member’s control, potentially after a Utility Member had begun incurring construction costs with the expectation of serving the HIL.  Third, the Commission stated that the current record suggested that Tri-State had not sufficiently justified the degree of discretion that it proposed to afford itself in implementing various aspects of its HIL proposal, such as in its evaluation criteria and in deciding whether loads should be aggregated.  
Fourth, the Commission noted its concern that the interactions between the proposed reliability criteria and transmission criteria were not explained in sufficient detail for the Commission to assess whether they are just and reasonable.  Finally, the Commission noted that Tri-State had not provided specificity regarding the circumstances under which it would directly assign the cost of “transmission upgrades” and interconnection facilities to Utility Members in order for the Commission to evaluate whether direct assignment is consistent with the Commission’s cost causation precedent.
Filing
Tri-State asserts that its current proposal addresses the Commission’s guidance and resolves the jurisdictional concerns the Commission identified in the Order Rejecting Initial Filing.  Tri-State states that its proposal is consistent with Commission policy governing transmission service requests, non-discrimination, and cost causation principles.  Tri-State further states that its proposal aligns with the Commission’s general approach to transmission planning and is modeled after large load programs established by other utilities.  
Tri-State proposes to establish a HIL Program in order to:  (1) facilitate the unprecedented level and pace of economic development across the Tri-State Utility Members’ systems; (2) limit the risk of stranded assets resulting from HIL integration, which could create financial risk for Tri-State and its Utility Members; and (3) continue to meet all resource planning and associated regulatory requirements.  Tri-State asserts that utilities are facing several risks in bringing large loads online and, to address the risks, Tri-State’s proposal incorporates HILs into its long-term forecast within a high impact load category in a manner that ensures all similarly situated Utility Members’ HIL projects are treated alike.  
Tri-State proposes a HIL Program consisting of a HIL Tariff and a pro forma HIL Agreement.  Tri-State proposes to define a HIL as load exceeding or forecasted to exceed 45 MW within four years and being served from a single Tri-State delivery point.     Tri-State maintains the biennial study cycle (HIL Cycle) beginning with a “kickoff” meeting with Utility Members and their potential HIL Customers.  Further, Tri-State proposes to require Utility Members to:  (1) complete a member project request form;    (2) pay the non-refundable HIL Evaluation Fee; (3) provide a copy of an executed MCHIL between the Utility Member and retail HIL Customer; and (4) agree to a HIL Agreement to be executed by the Utility Member and Tri-State to facilitate the responsibility for serving the HIL project.
The proposed HIL Program requires Utility Members to submit a Participation Package and non-refundable HIL Evaluation Fee of:  (1) $35,000 plus $1,000 per MW for HIL requests less than 80 MW; (2) $150,000 for HIL requests between 80 and                   200 MW; or (3) $250,000 for HIL requests above 200 MW.  Tri-State proposes to review the information provided in the Participation Package using resource plan modeling software that would analyze the load, the resources available to meet that load, and any environmental, reliability, or transmission constraints.  To confirm that Tri-State conducted the HIL evaluation process consistently with the terms of the HIL Tariff,             Tri-State proposes to employ an independent evaluator funded by the HIL Evaluation Fees to review the evaluation process of each HIL Cycle.  The independent evaluator would complete its review, using reasonable efforts, within 15 business days of the end of the Proposal Period or Revised Proposal Period.  Tri-State also proposes that its member system planning process includes performing a feasibility study at no cost to the Utility Member.  
Tri-State proposes to include HIL requests that pass the initial or revised load evaluation process in its transmission planning under the applicable OATT processes for transmission service.  Tri-State also proposes to follow the transmission cost allocation regime under the applicable OATT of each transmission provider needed to serve the Utility Member’s load.  Accordingly, to mitigate the cost and risk to Tri-State’s Utility Members not associated with a specific HIL request, Tri-State proposes to allocate directly to the Utility Member associated with a HIL request the cost of interconnection facilities and any directly assigned upgrades under an OATT.  The Utility Member may then choose to pass those costs directly to its HIL Customer.  To effectuate this arrangement, Tri-State proposes to use a Facilities Construction Agreement between itself and the participating Utility Member, which would be filed with the Commission.  Tri-State states that, to the extent that a HIL project with directly assigned costs is aggregated across multiple Utility Members, Tri-State will allocate such costs to each Utility Member on a pro rata basis.
To implement the HIL Program, Tri-State proposes a pro forma HIL Agreement that requires, among other things, that the Utility Member provide security in the amount of $1.869 million/MW.  Tri-State states that the proposed security is intended to help mitigate the risks to Tri-State’s other Utility Members if Tri-State is not paid the monthly minimum demand or energy requirements or if the HIL Agreement terminates early.   Tri-State also states that, because the HIL Customer’s proposed new load will trigger   Tri-State to acquire additional resources, Tri-State is obligated to pay for those resources regardless of the HIL Customer’s performance.  Tri-State explains that the proposed security amount reflects the financial commitments it must make to resource project developers to acquire resources to support HIL Customers.  Tri-State explains further that the proposed security will enable Tri-State to avoid socializing the risk of the HIL Customer’s under or non-performance across Tri-State’s entire membership.  Tri-State explains that the proposed security covers a “10-year period of generation demand costs to align with other utility’s approaches to high impact load and to balance protection by covering resource capacity costs across two-thirds of the HIL[] A[greement] term.” 
As part of the HIL Agreement, Tri-State proposes minimum billing demand and energy floors associated with serving HILs to Utility Members’ invoices to ensure a minimum level of cost recovery.  To accommodate varying types of HILs, Tri-State proposes to allow the Utility Member to select among two options of minimum demand and minimum energy charges:  (1) 90% Minimum Demand and 75% Minimum Energy or (2) 75% Minimum Demand and 50% Minimum Energy.  Tri-State proposes that the HIL Agreement have a 15-year minimum term, along with provisions related to early termination, monthly energy and demand projections, and load ramp projections (LRP).  Tri-State’s proposed HIL Agreement also requires a Utility Member to execute and provide a copy of a MCHIL. 
Tri-State proposes reliability and transmission criteria to evaluate whether a HIL project could adversely affect Tri-State’s system.  Tri-State states that the criteria are evaluated separately.  Specifically, Tri-State proposes two sets of reliability metrics for use in all resource planning modeling scenarios:  (1) a traditional planning reserve margin aimed at limiting loss of load to a one-day-in-ten-year threshold (Level 1 Reliability Metrics); and (2) planning for greater than 99% reliability during extreme weather events (Level 2 Reliability Metrics).  Tri-State asserts that all HIL projects would be evaluated against these reliability metrics as set forth in the most recent Tri-State resource plan on file with the Colorado Commission, and a project would have to pass both Level 1 and Level 2 Reliability Metrics to proceed.  Further, Tri-State’s proposed HIL Tariff includes an economic criterion to evaluate whether the HIL project is economically priced so as to avoid cost shifts and an increase in Tri-State’s Class A rate.  Tri-State states that the transmission evaluation criterion assesses Tri-State’s ability to procure necessary equipment and construct necessary interconnection facilities and network upgrades by the requested in-service date.  Tri-State explains that, unlike the reliability assessment, the transmission availability assessment is intended to focus on Tri-State’s ability to upgrade its system in time to allow delivery of the required power to the new delivery points without causing transmission facilities to operate outside design limits.  Tri-State states that there is no interaction between the reliability and transmission assessments because they rely on different models and analyze Tri-State’s system performance in different ways.
In response to the Commission’s concerns in the Order Rejecting Initial Filing, Tri-State describes events that could result in early termination of the HIL Agreement.  Those events include:  (1) a Utility Member or third party failing to establish security within 10 days of the security due date; (2) the project exceeding the maximum annual energy or maximum project peak demand twice in any four-year period; (3) the project exceeding the monthly energy or monthly demand in the LRP three or more times in any 12-month period; and (4) the termination of the MCHIL.  Tri-State also proposes that when the resource or transmission expenses exceed those used in the evaluation by 10% or more, the Utility Member has the option of either buying down the project by paying their portion of excess costs or terminating the HIL Agreement.  Tri-State also proposes provisions under which the project will be de-energized if it exceeds the maximum annual energy or maximum project peak demand, or the monthly energy or demand as stated in the LRP.  
Also, in response to the Commission’s concerns, Tri-State specifies that it proposes to aggregate smaller loads that collectively would qualify as a HIL to prevent Utility Members, or project developers, from circumventing the evaluation process.               Tri-State asserts that to prevent the perception of undue discretion, aggregation decisions in the proposed HIL Tariff are also made using specific criteria.  Further, Tri-State states that it will only aggregate loads “that are located within five physical miles of each other and (1) sharing one or more of the following:  common owner(s), a common parent company, common control; and (2) sharing one or more of the following:  common local electrical infrastructure, physical layout, character of service, and end use.”
Tri-State states that it serves its Eastern Interconnection Utility Members through an Eastern Interconnection wholesale power contract between Tri-State and Basin.                Tri-State explains that Basin may be developing its own program to serve large loads, which could be applicable to large loads in the Eastern Interconnection and could set a threshold lower than Tri-State’s 45 MW threshold. 
Notices and Responsive Pleadings
Notice of Tri-State’s filing was published in the Federal Register,                                      91 Fed. Reg. 15992 (Mar. 31, 2026), with interventions and protests due on or before April 16, 2026.  Timely motions to intervene were filed by:  Basin; Columbus Electric Cooperative, Inc.; Highline Electric Association; High Plains Power, Inc. (High Plains Power); K.C. Electric Association; Morgan County Rural Electric Association; Mountain View Electric Association, Inc.; Public Citizen, Inc.; San Isabel Electric Association, Inc.; Springer Electric Cooperative, Inc. (Springer); Tallgrass MLP Operations, LLC; White River Electric Association, Inc.; and the Wyoming Cooperatives.  Poudre Valley Rural Electric Association, Inc. (Poudre Valley) and Wheat Belt Public Power District (Wheat Belt) filed timely motions to intervene and protests.  Data Center Coalition filed a timely motion to intervene and comments.  On April 30, 2026, the Wyoming Cooperatives filed comments.  On May 6, 2026, Tri-State filed a motion for leave to answer and answer to Poudre Valley’s and Wheat Belt’s protests.  On May 12, 2026, High Plains Power filed a motion for leave to answer and answer to Tri-State’s May 6, 2026 answer.  On May 18, 2026, Tri-State filed a motion for leave to answer and answer to High Plains Power’s answer.  On May 19, 2026, Springer filed an answer to Tri-State’s May 6, 2026 answer.  On May 20, 2026, Poudre Valley filed a motion for leave to answer and answer to Tri-State’s May 6, 2026 and May 18, 2026 answers.  On May 20, 2026, Wheat Belt filed a motion for leave to answer and answer to Tri-State’s May 18, 2026 answer.
On May 22, 2026, a deficiency letter was issued requesting additional information regarding Tri-State’s filing (Deficiency Letter).  On June 16, 2026, Tri-State filed a response to the Deficiency Letter (Deficiency Response).  Notice of Tri-State’s Deficiency Response was published in the Federal Register, 91 Fed. Reg. 37102                   (June 22, 2026), with interventions and protests due on or before June 30, 2026.  Wheat Belt filed a protest.  On July 15, 2026, Tri-State filed a motion for leave to answer and answer to Wheat Belt’s protest. 
Comments, Protests, and Answers
Jurisdiction 
Data Center Coalition asserts that Tri-State’s proposed HIL Tariff “appears to remedy the jurisdictional defect that was the basis of the Commission’s rejection of the previous HIL Tariff.” 
Poudre Valley asserts that Tri-State’s proposal intrudes on retail rate regulation because the proposal still requires that Utility Members enter into a MCHIL with their large load customers with terms that comport with the HIL Agreement.  Poudre Valley contends that Tri-State’s proposal does indirectly what the Commission determined could not be done directly in the Order Rejecting Initial Filing.  Poudre Valley asserts that Tri-State Board Policy 121 encourages Utility Members to ensure that certain provisions comport with the HIL Agreement.  
Poudre Valley argues that Tri-State is redefining its obligation to provide full requirements service, wholesale power and transmission service, to its Utility Members by carving out an exception for the HIL and then “dictat[ing] terms of retail service by threatening not to serve HIL[s]” unless the Utility Member has a MCHIL with the retail customer that conforms with the HIL Tariff and HIL Agreement.  However, Poudre Valley states that Tri-State’s proposing requirements for HILs “is not per se unreasonable” and that it “also has no opposition to modifications to Tri-State’s planning process that would improve Tri-State’s ability to ‘evaluate the reliability, economic, and regulatory impacts’ of incorporating a HIL onto its system.”  Poudre Valley argues that “the threshold problem is that the HIL T[ariff] proposal redefines Tri-State’s obligation to serve its Members’ present and future requirements based on an arbitrary and unsupported determination of what constitutes a HIL.”    
In its answer, Tri-State argues that the HIL Tariff does not impose on retail rate regulation because the HIL Tariff imposes obligations only on Tri-State’s Utility Members and leaves those same Utility Members full discretion as to whether they will flow those terms through to their non-jurisdictional MCHILs.  Tri-State argues that the mere fact that the “HIL Tariff could have incidental effects at the retail level ‘is of no legal consequence’ because transactions that occur on the wholesale market have natural consequences at the retail level.”  Tri-State also argues that the purpose of the HIL Tariff is to ensure that Tri-State can responsibly serve all of its Utility Members’ loads in a timely and non-discriminatory manner, including HILs.  Tri-State states that its Utility Members and Tri-State have agreed they will follow Good Utility Practice in the performance of “all obligations” created by the WESCs.  Tri-State also notes that, in meeting the all-requirements obligation, Tri-State will adopt practices that include the evaluation criteria in the HIL Tariff (affordability, reliability, responsibility, and timing) consistent with Good Utility Practice.  
In response to Tri-State’s answer that it will adopt practices that include the evaluation criteria in the HIL Tariff consistent with Good Utility Practice, High Plains Power argues that inherent in Tri-State’s argument is the notion that an agreement to follow Good Utility Practice imposes an obligation on Utility Members to accept the terms and conditions of the HIL Tariff because of the agreement in Tri-State’s OATT to follow Good Utility Practice.  High Plains Power argues that Good Utility Practice does not encompass forbearance of concerns that are validly raised and urges the Commission not to create any new precedent suggesting that a Utility Member is bound by proposed tariff changes by virtue of Good Utility Practice.
Tri-State argues that High Plains Power misinterprets Tri-State’s response to Poudre Valley.  Tri-State asserts that the evaluation criteria used to determine whether a Utility Member’s HIL may successfully proceed through the HIL process is consistent with the criteria used to determine whether Tri-State has met its contractual obligation to serve load consistent with Good Utility Practice.  Tri-State argues that, contrary to High Plains Power’s argument, abiding by the Good Utility Practice standard does not impose some legal standard that prevents its Utility Members from protesting the terms of a proposed tariff.
In response to Tri-State’s answer, Springer expresses concern that rejecting Poudre Valley’s protest based on Tri-State’s Good Utility Practice standard argument would negatively impact the rights of the Utility Members to file a protest to any         Tri-State filing with the Commission.  Springer requests that the Commission reject this portion of Tri-State’s answer. 
Security
The Wyoming Cooperatives support Tri-State’s proposal, stating that it effectively balances Tri-State’s responsibility to reliably serve demand in accordance with Good Utility Practice.  Additionally, the Wyoming Cooperatives state that Tri-State’s proposal addresses cost allocation concerns and members’ native load growth requirements, while taking into account the operational and financial challenges associated with integrating large, potentially speculative demand.  The Wyoming Cooperatives assert that Tri-State’s proposal ensures that existing members are not required to subsidize costs incurred to serve a discrete, high-impact customer and have security to mitigate against excess capacity.
Poudre Valley and Wheat Belt argue that Tri-State fails to demonstrate that the proposed security requirements are just and reasonable and sized to mitigate the risks created by large loads to protect Utility Members.  Poudre Valley asserts that, in rejecting Tri-State’s initial proposal, the Commission encouraged Tri-State to include analysis to support a finding that the security requirement is appropriately sized to mitigate the risks of interconnecting HILs onto Tri-State’s system.  However, Poudre Valley argues,                 Tri-State provides no evidence to support its conclusion that the security requirement is appropriately sized to protect Utility Members from improper cost shifts.  Further, Poudre Valley explains that while Tri-State purports to justify its proposed                            $1.869 million/MW security proposal, the evidence presented by Tri-State witness Bradberry does not provide any justification but rather discusses the function of a security requirement in general terms, explains how the security is used in the HIL Agreement, and explains the details of the calculation used to derive the security.  Poudre Valley asserts that the Commission must find substantial evidence in the record to support a quantification of the risks of improper cost shifts and must analyze the               $1.869 million security proposal in light of that quantification to find that it is appropriately sized in relation to those risks.  
Poudre Valley also protests Tri-State’s use of a 10-year term in calculating the security requirement.  Poudre Valley argues that Tri-State’s claims that having resource contracts aligned with the minimum 15-year term of the HIL Agreement provides protection for the majority of the exposure to Utility Members by covering resource capacity costs for two-thirds of the HIL Agreement term does not justify the reasonableness of the 10-year term.  Further, Poudre Valley argues that Tri-State takes a leap of logic in assuming that the benefits and risks are appropriately balanced as a result of its proposal to cover resource capacity costs for two-thirds of the HIL Agreement term.  Poudre Valley asserts that, more importantly, Tri-State fails to demonstrate that use of the 10-year term to calculate the security requirement comports with the cost causation principle or results in wholesale rates that are just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory.  Poudre Valley also argues that Tri-State’s proposal to calculate the security requirement by multiplying the generation demand component of its 2026 Class A Rate of $15.58 per kW-month (after being converted to an annual charge) by a term of 10 years results in a double charge because the generation demand component of the 2026 Class A Rate is also a component of Tri-State’s minimum billing proposal.  
Data Center Coalition asserts that Tri-State’s security is still high compared to analogs at the state level.
In its answer, Tri-State asserts that Poudre Valley’s claim that Tri-State failed to demonstrate how a security based on a 10-year period is appropriately sized to mitigate the risks created by HILs is inaccurate, as it does not recognize the data-driven approach Tri-State adopted to establish the security period.  Further, Tri-State reiterates that its security requirements fit within the range of security requirements imposed by other utilities and was approved by the Tri-State Board of Directors.
45 MW Threshold
Poudre Valley argues that Tri-State fails to demonstrate that its 45 MW threshold is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory.  Poudre Valley explains that one of the factors Tri-State used in determining the threshold was historical load requests by Utility Members.  Poudre Valley asserts that Tri-State designated its analysis of historical load requests as confidential.  Poudre Valley argues that it did not execute the proposed protective agreement “because of concerns that a specific provision could prejudice Poudre Valley’s ability to meaningfully participate in this proceeding.”  Poudre Valley asserts that because it did not have access to the confidential information, it was deprived of the ability to analyze the size of load additions and modifications requested by Utility Members in recent years in order to better assess the 45 MW threshold.  Poudre Valley also questions the reasonableness of Tri-State defining a HIL as a load addition forecasted to exceed 45 MW within four years from the Utility Member’s request.  Poudre Valley argues that Tri-State provides no explanation as to why the period is appropriate.
Poudre Valley further argues that Tri-State fails to demonstrate how applying different size thresholds to Utility Members serving load in the Eastern Interconnection is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory.  Poudre Valley notes Tri-State’s claim that Basin may establish a 25 MW threshold that would apply to Tri-State’s Eastern Interconnection Utility Members.  Poudre Valley argues that if Tri-State applies different size thresholds to different Utility Members in the Eastern and Western Interconnections, Tri-State has not demonstrated how the different applications would not result in undue discrimination.  Poudre Valley also asserts that Tri-State applying a size threshold established by Basin to Eastern Interconnection Utility Members would violate the filed rate doctrine since Basin is not regulated by the Commission and therefore its size threshold is not established in a Commission-approved tariff. 
Wheat Belt argues that the 45 MW threshold does not reflect the realities of                 Tri-State’s membership because the 45 MW threshold is (1) double the peak loads of 10 of Tri-State’s 40 members, and (2) greater than or equal to the peak loads of more than half of Tri-State’s members.  However, Wheat Belt asserts that for some of Tri-State’s largest Utility Members, the threshold would be applicable to load additions that are equivalent to 16% to 33% of those members’ peak loads.  Wheat Belt states that it does not argue that it is inappropriate to apply terms and conditions that are unique to serving load additions of this magnitude for the larger Utility Members, but rather argues that it is unreasonable for Tri-State to adopt a threshold that would not apply the terms and conditions of the HIL program to load additions that are 100% of the peak loads of more than half of Tri-State’s Utility Members.  
In its answer, Tri-State argues that Wheat Belt’s assertion that the 45 MW threshold would not apply to load additions that are 100% or more of the peak loads of more than half of Tri-State’s Members is contradictory to the purpose of the HIL Tariff.  Specifically, Tri-State argues that the minimum MW threshold established for HILs is designed to support its Utility Members’ efforts to secure the advantages of HILs, while ensuring Tri-State is able to meet its obligations to serve the requirements of its Utility Members under the WESCs.  Tri-State asserts that a lower threshold would potentially require Utility Members with large loads that do not present the same reliability,                cross-subsidization, and regulatory risks to Tri-State’s system to unnecessarily navigate the HIL process, and would, therefore, be unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory.
Tri-State argues that the potential existence of different MW thresholds on the     Tri-State and Basin systems does not render either threshold unjust or unreasonable.            Tri-State explains that there is no single correct threshold since there is a “zone of reasonableness” within which thresholds can be set, and both Tri-State’s and Basin’s potential threshold fall within that zone, as represented by the range of thresholds utilized by other utilities.  Further, Tri-State states that the Commission recently accepted a tariff defining a large load as 50 MW.
Tri-State argues that its Eastern and Western Interconnection Utility Members are not similarly situated for the purposes of the proposed HIL Tariff because they operate in different interconnections and are subject to different resource planning processes, such that Tri-State’s Eastern Interconnection Utility Members may be required to comply with an additional tariff for the interconnection of large loads.  Tri-State explains that the difference in the resource planning required to serve HILs of Tri-State’s Eastern and Western Interconnection Utility Members is material, and provides a reasoned basis for the potential imposition of different MW thresholds for the HIL interconnection process, to the extent that Basin may determine it is necessary to ensure its system is capable of meeting its contractual commitments to serve Tri-State’s Eastern Interconnection Utility Members.
Tri-State disagrees with Poudre Valley’s assertions that Tri-State’s proposal for its Eastern and Western Interconnection Utility Members violates the filed rate doctrine.  Tri-State explains that it is not asking the Commission to accept terms and conditions for Eastern Interconnection Utility Members without the specificity required by the filed rate doctrine, but rather Tri-State is providing notice to its Utility Members and the Commission that different rules could apply for Eastern Interconnection Utility Members.
In response to Poudre Valley’s concerns about its inability to access confidential information, Tri-State explains that unknown technical issues prevented the delivery and/or receipt of email communications from Poudre Valley.  Tri-State states that the requested information has been provided to Poudre Valley and Poudre Valley has consented to Tri-State representing that it has resolved Poudre Valley’s concerns.
In its answer, Wheat Belt asserts that Tri-State’s HIL Tariff contains 26 individual references to Basin across multiple provisions and that these provisions clearly establish requirements that will apply to Eastern Interconnection Utility Members if the HIL Tariff is approved.  Wheat Belt argues that the HIL Tariff:  (1) seeks “pre-approval” for                     Tri-State to adopt any currently unknown terms that Basin may establish, and to impose those terms on Eastern Interconnection Utility Members; and (2) establishes contractual privity between Eastern Interconnection Utility Members and Basin such that Eastern Interconnection Utility Members will be obligated to comply with currently unknown terms that Basin may establish in the future.  Wheat Belt highlights the following sections of the HIL Tariff and HIL Agreement:  (1) section 3.6 of the HIL Tariff, which provides that “Basin’s requirements will be applicable to Utility Members in the Eastern Interconnection;” (2) section 4.B of the HIL Agreement, which provides that Eastern Interconnection Utility Members “will cooperate with Tri-State and Basin and provide any information or documentation required or requested by Basin;” and (3) section 7.B of the HIL Agreement, which provides that, “if the load of the Project is located in the Eastern Interconnection and served pursuant to the Basin East WPC, the Security Amount will be the amount of the Basin Security.”  Wheat Belt argues that accepting Tri-State’s proposal “pre-approving” provisions that will subject Eastern Interconnection Utility Members to currently unknown terms that Basin may establish is contrary to the requirements of the filed rate doctrine.  Wheat Belt also argues that, in seeking                     pre-approval of currently unknown terms, Tri-State is requesting the Commission delegate to Basin its exclusive jurisdiction over wholesale rates.
Wheat Belt also argues that Tri-State’s answer fails to rebut Wheat Belt’s assertion that the 45 MW threshold does not reflect the realities of Tri-State’s membership.  Wheat Belt reiterates that its protest of the 45 MW threshold focused on the concentrated risks posed by loads—not the diverse, diffuse nature of traditional load growth, as Tri-State suggests.  Wheat Belt argues that Tri-State’s failure to provide a credible basis for the               45 MW threshold is a critical defect.  Wheat Belt notes that while Tri-State claims a                45 MW threshold aligns with size thresholds in other programs and is consistent with Commission precedent (which uses proxy groups to establish reasonable rates),                     Tri-State’s answer is problematic because it assumes, rather than demonstrates, that the proxy group entities are similarly situated to Tri-State.  Further, Wheat Belt argues that the HIL Tariff diminishes Tri-State’s service obligation because it carves out HILs as a sub-set of Utility Members’ requirements that Tri-State may not be obligated to serve.  Wheat Belt asserts that the HIL Tariff redefines Tri-State’s service obligation by affording different treatment to HILs as compared to other loads.
HIL Cycle
The Wyoming Cooperatives assert that the HIL Tariff is essential to economic development in Wyoming.  Specifically, the Wyoming Cooperatives emphasize that HIL projects can translate into tangible benefits for Wyoming—including construction activity, long-term jobs, local tax base expansion, and broader economic development—if the Wyoming Members can respond on the timelines demanded by large load customers.  The Wyoming Cooperatives state that rejection of the HIL Tariff would inject uncertainty into Tri-State’s ability to offer a clear, Commission-approved service construct for HILs, leading to the loss of projects to competing jurisdictions and providers.
Poudre Valley argues that the HIL Cycle provides no flexibility for studying projects that may come up in between HIL Cycles and therefore creates a realistic possibility that Utility Members will miss opportunities to serve HILs.  Poudre Valley asserts that other public utilities have more flexible study periods; for example, SPP accepts requests at any time.  The Wyoming Cooperatives state that Tri-State’s HIL Tariff sets clear service conditions for HILs and provides a predictable process for planning, interconnection, and resource procurement.  
In its answer, Tri-State argues that Poudre Valley’s assertion that the HIL Cycle is arbitrary and inflexible ignores Tri-State’s stated reasons for establishing the planning HIL Cycle altogether.  Specifically, Tri-State asserts that Poudre Valley makes no attempt to argue that the HIL Cycle fails to satisfy the just and reasonable standard.  
Deficiency Letter, Deficiency Response, and Protest
The Deficiency Letter asked Tri-State to explain why the WPC requires                      Tri-State’s Utility Members to meet any and all obligations from Basin and to explain why these obligations are just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.  In response, Tri-State explains that its WPC with Basin does not require       Tri-State’s Utility Members to meet any and all obligations from Basin, but rather                Tri-State and Basin, as the parties to the WPC, are required to fulfill the obligations and receive the benefits of the contract in accordance with the terms and conditions therein.  Tri-State asserts that the WPC does raise the possibility that the terms under which              Tri-State serves its Eastern Interconnection Utility Members could be different from the terms that apply in the Western Interconnection.  Tri-State states that if Basin imposes terms that impact Tri-State’s Eastern Interconnection Utility Members’ HILs differently from its Western Interconnection Utility Members’ HILs—for example, a different minimum threshold for a HIL Customer—that difference alone would not cause the               pro forma HIL Agreement to be unjust and unreasonable or result in undue discrimination or preferential treatment.  Tri-State notes that the Commission has recognized that discrimination or preference for either Eastern or Western Interconnection Utility Members is allowed, referencing the Contract Termination Payment (CTP) and BYOR proceedings.   
Tri-State further explains that the application of different terms to its Eastern and Western Interconnection Utility Members’ HILs does not create undue discrimination or preferential treatment.  Tri-State asserts that the Commission has already recognized the differences between serving Tri-State’s Utility Members’ Eastern and Western Interconnection loads, and has found that differing treatment of Utility Members based on the cost structure of resources serving a load location can be just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.  Tri-State states that these differences were driven by the Commission’s conclusion that Tri-State’s chosen resource to meet its service obligations in the Eastern Interconnection, the Basin WPC, required a different CTP methodology.  Tri-State contends that since the Commission approved distinct treatment for Eastern Interconnection Utility Members under Tri-State’s BYOR tariff, and the Commission specifically accepted Tri-State’s ability to “flow through” the requirements of Basin’s HIL tariffs, the Commission should accept the same treatment in this proceeding.  Tri-State explains that the proposed HIL Tariff’s treatment of                     Tri-State’s Eastern Interconnection Utility Members’ loads follows the Commission’s directives related to the Basin WPC and the different service conditions that exist within the two interconnections, such as the different financial risk and debt that Tri-State undertakes in the Western Interconnection.
In addition, the Deficiency Letter asked Tri-State to explain:  (1) how Tri-State will determine whether a future Commission filing will be necessary; and (2) to the extent Basin proposes to impose terms and conditions on Eastern Interconnection Utility Members, whether Tri-State would specify those terms and conditions in its tariff through a future filing under FPA section 205.  Tri-State responds that under any circumstance where Basin is unwilling or unable to serve a Tri-State Utility Member’s HIL in the Eastern Interconnection on terms materially consistent with Tri-State’s proposed                  pro forma HIL Agreement, then Tri-State will file a non-conforming HIL Agreement with the Commission for review.  Tri-State states that the only circumstance where a filing may not be necessary is where Basin proposes to impose a less stringent requirement than that in Tri-State’s proposed pro forma HIL Agreement, but the Eastern Interconnection Utility Member voluntarily chooses to abide by the standard requirement set forth in the pro forma HIL Agreement.  
The Deficiency Letter asked Tri-State whether the provisions relating to Eastern Interconnection Utility Members intended to incorporate by reference any current or future requirements promulgated by Basin.  Tri-State responds that they are not and explains that any requirement or non-conforming term that Basin proposes to impose on an Eastern Interconnection Utility Member’s HIL would be included in a non-conforming HIL Agreement filed with the Commission.
The Deficiency Letter asked Tri-State to explain whether the amount of the Basin security is limited or constrained by any of the terms and conditions of the HIL Tariff.  Tri-State responds that it is not limited and that Tri-State would require the same security amount from an Eastern Interconnection Utility Member that Basin requires of Tri-State without any additional markup or administrative fee.  Tri-State states that if the Basin security amount is less than Tri-State’s security amount, the Eastern Interconnection Utility Member would pay the lower amount, which would be reflected in a non-conforming HIL Agreement filed with the Commission, as explained below.  Tri-State explains that the proposed HIL Tariff’s security amount is intended to protect Tri-State’s other Utility Members from cost shifts, and that it is appropriate for the Utility Member to pay only the security amount Tri-State requires to avoid cross-subsidization, consistent with the general principle of cost causation.  
The Deficiency Letter asked Tri-State to explain how the Basin security would be implemented, and whether Tri-State would give notice of the Basin security to the Eastern Interconnection Utility Member prior to execution of the HIL Agreement.       Tri-State responds that it will provide notice to an Eastern Interconnection Utility Member upon receipt of any security requirements from Basin and before filing a       non-conforming HIL Agreement with the Commission.  Tri-State states that the filed rate doctrine would prevent Tri-State from requiring payment from a Utility Member for a security amount that was not previously authorized by the Commission.
The Deficiency Letter asked Tri-State to explain whether the Eastern Interconnection Utility Member would be subject to additional financial commitments after the execution of a HIL Agreement to the extent Basin modified its security requirements.  Tri-State responds that, prior to requesting security from an Eastern Interconnection Utility Member, Tri-State will seek to enter into an agreement with Basin that defines and describes all security requirements and procedures and financial conditions that are material to the proposed HIL Tariff.  Tri-State explains that, to date, neither it nor Basin has engaged in negotiations for such an agreement, and Tri-State has no information suggesting Basin plans to include security provisions in a future tariff or adopt or review any board policies that may impact the security amount.  Tri-State concludes that, notwithstanding any uncertainty regarding Basin’s future plans, Tri-State will include any modifications to the security amount in the pro forma HIL Agreement, a non-conforming HIL Agreement, or the filing of an Eastern HIL Tariff or ad hoc member-specific HIL Tariff for submission to the Commission.
Tri-State states that it believes its Deficiency Response demonstrates that its proposed HIL Tariff and pro forma HIL Agreement are just and reasonable.  However, Tri-State states that, if the Commission continues to have concerns about the treatment of Tri-State’s Eastern Interconnection Utility Members’ loads and Western Interconnection Utility Members’ loads, Tri-State offers an alternative proposal consisting of a HIL Tariff and pro forma HIL Agreement that would apply to Tri-State’s Western Interconnection Utility Members’ HILs (Alternative Western Interconnection HIL Tariff).  Tri-State explains that under its alternative proposal, if a Utility Member seeks service for a HIL in the Eastern Interconnection, then Tri-State, the Eastern Interconnection Utility Member, and Basin would determine if revisions to the proposed Alternative Western Interconnection HIL Tariff and/or pro forma HIL Agreement are necessary to meet specific service requirements from Basin, and if so, Tri-State would file the agreement with the Commission for review.  
Tri-State requests an effective date of July 16, 2026, for Commission approval of its proposed HIL Tariff and pro forma HIL Agreement, or as soon thereafter as the Commission finds appropriate, and the same effective date to the extent that the Commission instead requires a compliance filing for Tri-State’s Alternative Western Interconnection HIL Tariff and pro forma HIL Agreement.
In its protest to the Deficiency Response, Wheat Belt argues that Tri-State’s proposed Alternative Western Interconnection HIL Tariff creates new problems and fails to resolve pre-existing problems that render the proposed HIL Tariff unjust and unreasonable and unduly discriminatory.  
First, Wheat Belt argues that Tri-State’s proposed Alternative Western Interconnection HIL Tariff creates uncertainty as to which terms, if any, apply to             Tri-State’s Eastern Interconnection Utility Members’ HILs.  Wheat Belt avers that it serves load in both interconnections, so its customers cannot be certain they are not being discriminated against in one interconnection as compared to the other.
Second, Wheat Belt argues that Tri-State’s proposed Alternative Western Interconnection HIL Tariff is unduly discriminatory because it affords different treatment to similarly situated Utility Members.  Wheat Belt disagrees with Tri-State’s comparison of the treatment of Tri-State’s Utility Members in the Eastern and Western Interconnections under its proposed Alternative Western Interconnection HIL Tariff treatment and the CTP.  Wheat Belt argues that in developing the CTP, the Commission started from the premise that exit fees should be based on the costs Tri-State incurred to serve the withdrawing Utility Member, and because Tri-State may incur different costs to serve Utility Members in the Eastern and Western Interconnections, different treatment should be allowed.  Wheat Belt argues that the impact of interconnecting large loads is a different issue than the costs incurred to serve a withdrawing Utility Member.  Wheat Belt further argues that Tri-State has not demonstrated that a new 45 MW load has a different impact in the Eastern Interconnection compared to the Western Interconnection. 
Third, Wheat Belt argues that Tri-State continues to offer no basis for the 45 MW threshold.  Wheat Belt contends that since articulating its concerns about the 45 MW threshold, the Commission established size thresholds that depend on the voltage at which the large load interconnects to the transmission system, and while Wheat Belt is not necessarily endorsing these approaches, it believes that the rationale underlying them is the type of granular approach Tri-State should have taken when proposing its 45 MW threshold.   
In its answer to Wheat Belt’s protest, Tri-State argues that Wheat Belt raises no new issues.  Moreover, Tri-State reiterates that the HIL Tariff appropriately differentiates between Eastern and Western Interconnection Utility Member loads based on legitimate operational, planning, and contractual differences, consistent with Commission and judicial precedent.  Tri-State further defends its proposed 45 MW threshold for defining HILs as well supported in the record and aligned with similar Commission-approved thresholds.
Discussion
Procedural Matters
Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 
18 C.F.R. § 385.214 (2025), the timely, unopposed motions to intervene serve to make the entities that filed them parties to this proceeding.
Rule 213(a)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 
18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2) (2025), prohibits an answer to a protest or answer unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority.  We accept the answers filed by Tri-State, High Plains Power, Springer, Poudre Valley, and Wheat Belt because they have provided information that assisted us in our decision-making process.
Substantive Matters
As discussed below, we find Tri-State’s proposed HIL Tariff and pro forma HIL Agreement to be just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential and, therefore, accept them, subject to condition, effective July 16, 2026, and direct Tri-State to submit a compliance filing within 30 days of the date of this order.
We find that Tri-State’s proposed HIL Tariff and pro forma HIL Agreement are a just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential approach to addressing the operational and planning challenges associated with rapid additions of large loads.  As explained below, Tri-State’s proposed HIL Tariff and pro forma HIL Agreement will help Tri-State to maintain the reliable operation of its transmission system and provision of full requirements service to its Utility Members while also helping to protect against cost shifts to other Utility Members.  
Jurisdiction
The FPA authorizes the Commission to regulate “the sale of electric energy at wholesale in interstate commerce,” including both wholesale electricity rates and any rule or practice directly “affecting” such rates.  But the law places beyond the Commission’s jurisdiction, and leaves to the states alone, the regulation of “any other sale”—most notably, any retail sale—of electricity.  Section 201 of the FPA also explains that the Commission’s jurisdiction is limited to “those matters which are not subject to regulation by the states.”
Tri-State’s proposal governs the terms and conditions for full requirements service, which includes the provision of transmission service and wholesale power to   Tri-State’s Utility Members, and does not dictate the terms or conditions of retail service through the MCHIL.  We therefore find that the proposed HIL Tariff does not raise the same jurisdictional concerns as Tri-State’s initial filing in Docket No. ER25-3316-000, which the Commission rejected.  We also find that, because Tri-State’s proposal does not include provisions that establish terms or conditions of retail service in the MCHIL between the Utility Member and its retail customer (i.e., the HIL Customer), Tri-State’s proposal does not present an impermissible intrusion on retail rate regulation.  
We are not persuaded by Poudre Valley’s argument that Tri-State’s proposal represents an impermissible intrusion upon retail rate regulation.  The Commission rejected Tri-State’s prior proposal because it dictated terms of retail service between the Utility Member and its end-use load via mandatory terms in the MCHIL.  By comparison, Tri-State’s modified proposal cures this jurisdictional defect because it does not mandate specific terms or conditions in the MCHIL, and instead establishes terms of Tri-State’s pro forma HIL Agreement that apply to its Utility Members.  Moreover, the terms of the pro forma HIL Agreement on which Poudre Valley focuses, such as those relating to energy demand and collateral, pertain to the terms and conditions for Commission-jurisdictional full requirements service from Tri-State to its Utility Members, not retail service.  
For the same reasons, we are unpersuaded by Poudre Valley’s argument that               Tri-State’s proposal exceeds the Commission’s jurisdiction because Tri-State’s “encouragement” that members include MCHIL provisions that are consistent with HIL requirements functionally dictates they do so.  Tri-State’s revised proposal does not dictate retail terms of service via the MCHIL, and Tri-State’s “encouragement” does not convert permissible Commission-jurisdictional requirements into impermissible retail terms and conditions.  Finally, even if those requirements could affect the HIL Customer, the United States Supreme Court has explained that the spheres of federal and state authority over electricity are not “hermetically sealed” from one another and that the Commission’s exercise of its regulatory oversight “does not run afoul” of FPA                   section 201 “just because it affects—even substantially —the quantity or terms of retail sales.”    We are not persuaded by Poudre Valley’s and Wheat Belt’s arguments that the HIL Tariff redefines Tri-State’s obligations to its Utility Members because the WESCs clearly set forth the obligations of Tri-State and Utility Members for full requirements service and allow modifications to those full requirements service contracts as specified.  Additionally, because we do not reject Poudre Valley’s protest based upon the Good Utility Practice standard arguments, we find High Plains Power’s and Springer’s protests are moot. 
Tri-State Has Addressed the Commission’s Prior Concerns
We also find that Tri-State’s proposal adequately addresses the other concerns the Commission identified in the Order Rejecting Initial Filing.  
First, that order found that Tri-State’s initial filing had not sufficiently demonstrated that the proposed security deposit was appropriately sized to mitigate the risks that Tri-State identified and that Tri-State had not explained why it is appropriate to round up its cost-based rate in deriving the security deposit.  In the instant filing,              Tri-State proposes a security deposit of $1.869 million/MW, explaining that the amount is based on the cost-based generation demand charge included in its recent Commission approved A-41 Rate over a 10-year period.  We find that the proposed security amount strikes a just and reasonable balance of allowing its Utility Members access to the HIL program to meet the needs of prospective HIL Customers and mitigating risks to other Utility Members because Tri-State must pay for additional resources to support the HIL project regardless of the HIL Customer’s performance.  While Data Center Coalition notes that Tri-State’s proposed security deposit remains on the higher end of the range used by other utilities, we find the proposal is just and reasonable given Tri-State’s explanation of how the proposed security deposit corresponds to Tri-State’s actual financial exposure if a Utility Member defaults or the HIL Agreement terminates early.  Specifically, Tri-State’s proposal ties the amount of the security deposit directly to the minimum-billing obligations in the HIL Agreement, which reflect the costs Tri-State must commit to support a HIL project.  Thus, we are not persuaded by Poudre Valley’s and Wheat Belt’s arguments that Tri-State has not sufficiently supported its proposed security deposit.
Second, in the Order Rejecting Initial Filing, the Commission found that Tri-State had not sufficiently explained why the HIL Agreement termination provisions would allow Tri-State to terminate a Utility Member’s HIL Agreement for reasons beyond the Utility Member’s control, potentially after a Utility Member had begun incurring construction costs with the expectation of serving the HIL.  We find that Tri-State’s proposal appropriately addresses the Commission’s concern because the early-termination provisions are now tied to clearly defined and objectively measurable conditions, and Tri-State provides a mechanism for the Utility Member to prevent termination when project costs increase after the HIL Cycle.  By allowing a Utility Member to “buy down” any increase in resource or transmission costs such that other Utility Members remain held harmless, the proposal ensures that a HIL Agreement will not be cancelled solely because of changing system conditions or updated planning results with no recourse for the Utility Member.  
Third, in the Order Rejecting Initial Filing, the Commission stated that Tri-State had not sufficiently justified the degree of discretion that it proposed to afford itself in implementing various aspects of its HIL proposal, such as in its evaluation criteria and in deciding whether loads should be aggregated.  We find that Tri-State’s proposal addresses the Commission’s concerns.  Tri-State specifies that it will aggregate loads only if they are within five physical miles of one another and meet the following criteria:  (1) sharing one or more elements such as common ownership, a common parent company, or common control; and (2) sharing one or more aspects including local electrical infrastructure, physical layout, character of service, or end use.  As such, we find that Tri-State has proposed to establish clear and transparent criteria that Tri-State will use to determine when to aggregate loads for purposes of its HIL Tariff.  
Fourth, in the Order Rejecting Initial Filing, the Commission noted that the interactions between the proposed reliability criterion and transmission criterion were not explained in sufficient detail for the Commission to assess whether they are just and reasonable.  We find that, here, Tri-State sufficiently supports these two criteria as just and reasonable and demonstrates that there is no interaction between them.  Specifically, Tri-State explains that the reliability criterion involves the assessment of two levels of reliability metrics to ensure that Tri-State has sufficient resources to meet demand.  Tri-State further explains that, in contrast, the transmission criterion assesses Tri-State’s ability to procure necessary equipment and construct necessary interconnection facilities and network upgrades by the requested in-service date.  Unlike the reliability assessment, Tri-State states, the transmission availability assessment is intended to focus on transmission issues, including thermal, voltage, and stability limits, and Tri-State’s ability to deliver the required power to the new delivery points without causing transmission facilities to operate outside their design limits.  Moreover, under                 Tri-State’s proposed HIL Tariff, Tri-State will evaluate HIL requests against these criteria using separate analyses that rely on different models, inputs, and decision criteria.  Therefore, we agree with Tri-State’s assertion that the reliability criterion and the transmission criterion do not interact within the evaluation process because each functions as an independent screening requirement that must be satisfied on its own terms.
We also find that Tri-State addresses the Commission’s concern that the reliability criterion lacks the necessary details for the Commission to evaluate its effectiveness and whether it ensures not unduly discriminatory treatment across projects through the addition of a clearer description of the reliability metrics to its HIL Tariff.  Specifically, Tri-State explains that the reliability criterion involves the assessment of two levels of reliability metrics as analyzed through the resource planning model:  (1) a traditional one-day-in-ten-year loss of load scenario; and (2) planning for greater than 99% reliability during extreme weather events.  With this additional detail, we find that Tri-State’s proposed reliability criterion for evaluating HIL requests is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.  Specifically, we find that              Tri-State’s proposal will ensure that Tri-State adheres to the reliability metrics in its ERP as required by the Colorado Commission, the criterion is clearly defined in the Tariff, and an independent evaluator will verify that the criterion has been applied consistently.   
Finally, in the Order Rejecting Initial Filing, the Commission noted that Tri-State had not provided specificity regarding the circumstances under which it would directly assign the cost of “transmission upgrades and interconnection facilities” to Utility Members in order for the Commission to evaluate whether direct assignment is consistent with the Commission’s cost causation precedent.  Here, Tri-State clarifies that it proposes to allocate the cost of interconnection facilities and any additional network upgrades that a transmission provider directly assigns to Tri-State Merchant to the Utility Member, who may elect to pass those costs directly to its HIL Customer.  Tri-State states that, to the extent that a HIL project with directly assigned costs is aggregated across multiple Utility Members, Tri-State will allocate such costs to each Utility Member on a pro rata basis.  We find that Tri-State’s additional explanation adequately demonstrates how the provision aligns with the Commission’s cost causation precedent because it will ensure that any costs that Tri-State Merchant is directly assigned to provide full requirements service to a Utility Member with a HIL Customer are borne by that Utility Member.
Protestors’ Concerns
We are not persuaded by the protesters’ concerns with the 45 MW threshold and HIL Cycle.  First, we find that Tri-State has demonstrated that its proposed 45 MW threshold is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.  As                    Tri-State explains, its proposed threshold coincides with recent large load requests                Tri-State has received from its Utility Members ranging from 45 MW to 650 MW in the first year.  We find that Tri-State’s proposal to establish its threshold in part based on an analysis of the size of load additions and modifications requested by Utility Members in recent years is reasonable.  Moreover, we find persuasive Tri-State’s explanation that it established its proposed 45 MW threshold in part because new resources to serve large loads, such as a gas generating unit, are typically 40 MW per turbine and take significant time to develop.  In response to Wheat Belt’s protest, we find that the MW threshold does not need to be tied to a Utility Member’s peak load size and that Tri-State reasonably justifies its proposed 45 MW threshold on the basis of the difficulty of procuring additional generation to serve a load of that magnitude.  We further note that there may be more than one just and reasonable proposal as to what the threshold for defining a high impact load should be, but that Tri-State has adequately supported its proposed 45 MW threshold in the instant filing.  
Further, we are not persuaded by Poudre Valley’s assertion that Tri-State’s instant proposal provides no flexibility for studying HIL projects that may come up in between HIL Cycles and therefore creates a realistic possibility that Utility Members will miss opportunities to serve HIL Customers.  We find that Tri-State’s proposed HIL Cycle provides a reasonable timeframe for Tri-State to conduct solicitations for new resources and identify any interconnection facilities and/or network upgrades necessary to provide full requirements service to Utility Members seeking to serve HIL Customers while not unreasonably delaying the provision of that service.
We also disagree with Poudre Valley’s and Wheat Belt’s arguments that                      Tri-State’s possible application of different thresholds in the Eastern and Western Interconnections is unduly discriminatory and violates the filed rate doctrine.  
At the outset, we find Tri-State’s proposal to apply two different MW thresholds for large loads in the Eastern and Western Interconnections in the event that Basin establishes a threshold lower than 45 MWs under a future large load tariff of its own is not unduly discriminatory.  Tri-State serves its Eastern Interconnection Utility Members through a wholesale power contract with Basin for full requirements service.  Because Basin plans and manages the resources and transmission systems to serve Tri-State’s Eastern Interconnection Utility Members, Basin’s policies and rates are applicable.  We find that applying two different thresholds would not be unduly discriminatory in this case because the Utility Members in the Eastern and Western Interconnections are not similarly situated.  
Further, we find that Tri-State has sufficiently explained how differences in the security amount between Basin and Tri-State will be handled.  Tri-State specifies that Eastern Interconnection Utility Members will pay the security amount Basin requires of Tri-State, with no markup or administrative fee.  Further, any non-conforming security amounts would be subject to Commission review because of Tri-State’s commitment to file them in a non-conforming HIL Agreement.  
We also disagree with Poudre Valley’s and Wheat Belt’s framing of Tri-State’s proposal as a “pre-approval” of unknown terms that may be imposed by Basin on                 Tri-State’s Eastern Interconnection Utility Members’ HILs, including the imposition of a different security amount.  The HIL Tariff provisions serve to clarify which tariff requirements apply to Eastern and Western Interconnection Utility Members.  As                  Tri-State explains, if Basin imposes terms that differ from those Tri-State proposes in its HIL Tariff, then Tri-State will submit a non-conforming HIL Agreement for Commission review.  We find that so long as Tri-State submits a non-conforming HIL Agreement for Commission review under such circumstances, then Tri-State’s HIL Tariff would not improperly incorporate by reference any future requirements promulgated by Basin.  That said, we also find that the proposed HIL Tariff language does not yet reflect Tri-State’s commitment in its Deficiency Response to file a non-conforming HIL Agreement under any such circumstances.  Accordingly, we direct Tri-State to file, within 30 days of the date of this order, a compliance filing adding language into the HIL Tariff that memorializes this commitment.  
For similar reasons, we find that Tri-State’s proposal does not violate the filed rate doctrine.  The proposed HIL Tariff and proposed pro forma HIL Agreement the Commission is approving in this order will be the rate.  Tri-State has committed to file any non-conforming HIL Agreement for the Commission’s review and approval, and    Tri-State’s compliance filing will formally incorporate that commitment into its HIL Tariff.  Because any change to the rate on file will be effectuated only prospectively and only after notice, we perceive no present or future problem related to the filed rate doctrine.
We are not persuaded by Poudre Valley’s assertion that Tri-State’s proposed security deposit and minimum billing represent an impermissible double charge.  As Tri-State notes, the purpose of the security deposit is as “collateral [] intended to help mitigate the risks to Tri-State’s other members if Tri-State is not paid the monthly minimum demand or energy requirements[,] or the [HIL Agreement] is terminated early.”   The security deposit is collateral on which Tri-State can draw if the Utility Member fails to satisfy the minimum billing requirements under the HIL Agreement, and if the Utility Member meets those requirements, its security deposit will be returned over the last nine years of service under that agreement.  As such, we find that Tri-State’s proposed security deposit and minimum billing requirements are not a double charge. 
Finally, we find Poudre Valley’s concerns regarding access to the information that Tri-State filed as non-public to be moot because the information has since been provided to Poudre Valley.    
The Commission orders:
(A)	Tri-State’s proposed HIL Tariff and pro forma HIL Agreement are hereby accepted, subject to condition, effective July 16, 2026, as requested, as discussed in the body of this order.
(B)	Tri-State is hereby directed to submit a compliance filing within 30 days of the date of this order, as discussed in the body of this order.
